articles.title: BC's new premier lucked into the job in an unexpected political turn
articles.summary: An electoral gamble by the Canadian province's outgoing premier, David Eby,  backfired as the provincial Conservatives take power for the first time since 1928.
articles.body:
A relative outsider has been elected the new leader of the Canadian province of British Columbia after the provincial Conservatives swept to power in a snap election.

Lorne Doerkson, who took the helm of the party just weeks ago, will be British Columbia's new premier after the Conservatives won a majority of seats in the legislative assembly. It's the first time the party has won in the province in nearly a century.

Outgoing Premier David Eby, of the New Democratic Party (NDP), called the snap election last month - two years early - in an attempt to shore up power for his party.

Eby's gamble backfired in what has become the province's biggest political shakeup in decades.

A former rodeo announcer and newspaper publisher, Doerkson was first elected to the British Columbia (BC) Legislative Assembly in 2020.

But the 58-year-old was surprised himself when he found out, while on a flight home from South Africa last month, that his caucus colleagues wanted him as the party's new figurehead.

The news came shortly after the former leader of the BC Conservatives, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned in September due to internal party conflict that saw a third of her caucus quit the party.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," Doerkson said in an interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC earlier this month.

Eby, who became premier in 2022, sought to take advantage of the divided BC Conservatives by calling the snap election.

He said the western Canadian province needed a "fire break" against US President Donald Trump's economic attacks and "Trump-style politics that threaten to infect" the province.

He defended his early election call by arguing his left-leaning party needed a bigger majority in the assembly to get its policies passed more quickly and easily.

"A one-seat majority meant every single vote could bring down the government," he said in a campaign video.

But Saturday's election results show voters were ready for someone new.

The NDP is projected to have won just 27 of the 93 total seats, while Doerkson's Conservatives are projected to have won 64.

"British Columbians are hardworking, trailblasing people," Doerkson said in his victory speech Saturday night. "They want a fair shot at building something in this province."

That "trailblasing spirit", he said, "just needs government that's on its side."

Doerkson has promised to cut red tape "like it's never been cut before" by fast-tracking forestry and mining permits, and to triple natural gas production by 2035.

Eby resigned as provincial NDP leader in his concession speech, and said he accepts "full responsibility" for the outcome.

The provincial Conservative win comes after another recent shakeup in Canadian provincial politics when earlier this month, Quebec's sovereigntist Parti Quebecois won enough seats in the provincial election to form a minority government, adding a new test for Canada's unity .

articles.title: Kenya bus crash kills at least 24 as government vows road safety crackdown
articles.summary: Church mourners die on Kenya’s Nairobi-Mombasa Highway weeks after another crash killed 17 people.
articles.body:
A bus carrying mourners has collided with a truck on a major highway in southeastern Kenya , killing at least 24 people, police say.

The crash happened in the Kanga area near Mtito Andei, on the road linking the capital, Nairobi, to the coastal city of Mombasa, at about 7:45am (04:45 GMT) on Sunday, October 25.

Another 24 people were injured, hospital officials said.

The deaths came just over three weeks after another crash on the highway killed 17 people, prompting fresh government promises to improve road safety.

The bus belonged to Power of the Word Church International in Mombasa and was taking passengers home from their pastor’s funeral in western Kenya.

They had stopped for breakfast shortly before the collision, according to one survivor.

The other vehicle was a truck transporting cement.

Violet Mwandonyi, who survived the crash, told the Associated Press on Sunday that she remembered passengers crying out for passing motorists to help.

She said she did not know what had happened to her two children, who had been travelling on the bus.

The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

Makueni County Commissioner Abdullahi Khalif, the government’s senior administrator in the area, told Kenyan newspaper The Standard that the bus driver had tried to overtake several vehicles before colliding with an oncoming truck.

Kenya’s National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) also identified dangerous overtaking as a possible cause. Another survivor said the truck struck the bus from behind.

On October 3, a crash involving several vehicles killed 17 people , most of them Catholic pilgrims travelling to a prayer site, near Salama on the same highway.

Police said a truck driver had tried to overtake another truck before the collision.

The NTSA had identified that stretch of road as an area with a history of crashes.

President William Ruto offered condolences on Sunday and ordered inspections of vehicles used for public transport.

Transport Minister Davis Chirchir said the government would step up enforcement against speeding and unsafe overtaking, improve dangerous sections of road and strengthen training and checks for commercial drivers.

In a statement on Sunday, Chirchir said the government would work with police, local authorities and lawmakers on the measures, including closer oversight of buses and heavy goods vehicles.

“We cannot continue treating road safety as business as usual,” he said, calling for stronger action to reduce deaths.

Figures from the NTSA, reported by Kenyan media, show that 5,009 people died in road crashes in 2025, with 2,150 deaths recorded in the first half of 2026.

The authority estimates that about 20,000 crashes occur across Kenya each year.

Following Sunday’s collision, it called for road crashes to be declared a national disaster.

articles.title: Woman busted in NYC rabbi syringe attack allegedly stabbed another Jewish man hours earlier: report
articles.summary: Anna Mochalova allegedly stalked a rabbi before stabbing him with a syringe in Manhattan's Diamond District, hours after allegedly attacking another man.
articles.body: A Brooklyn woman allegedly attacked two men in Midtown Manhattan before asking a third whether he was Jewish and walking away when he said he was Muslim, according to a criminal complaint. Anna Mochalova, 32, was arrested Saturday evening, police confirmed to Fox News Digital. She now faces hate crime charges in the attacks, which occurred five minutes apart, according to the complaint, and left one man hospitalized and another with a cut to his forearm. Manhattan Shomrim Safety Patrol credited its volunteers, the NYPD’s Hate Crimes Task Force, Shomrim groups in Crown Heights and Queens, and tips from the public with helping secure the arrest. MAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT, HATE CRIMES AFTER ALLEGEDLY DISRUPTING SHABBAT SERVICES AT NYC SYNAGOGUE "The suspect wanted for Wednesday’s two hate crime assaults in Midtown Manhattan is now in custody," the group wrote on X. The arrest followed a public appeal from Manhattan Shomrim seeking witnesses and security camera, dashcam or cellphone video from the Diamond District. BRONX MAN ACCUSED OF ATTACKING SHABBAT WORSHIPPERS ADMITTED MOTIVE IN RECORDED INTERVIEW, FEDS SAY The criminal complaint, provided to Fox News Digital by the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office, places the first attack outside 15 W. 47th St. around 5:50 p.m. Wednesday. A man dressed in traditional Hasidic Jewish clothing told investigators a woman approached him and began following him, continuing across the street when he tried to get away. Cornered against a vehicle, he felt a sharp, stinging sensation in his lower back, according to the complaint. He suffered a cut, bleeding and substantial pain. Police said the 26-year-old was taken to Bellevue Hospital in stable condition. NY ASSEMBLYMAN CALLS FOR DOJ TO INVESTIGATE MAMDANI, PROTECT JEWISH NEW YORKERS AFTER STABBING ATTACKS About five minutes later, a man wearing a yarmulke was waiting to cross at Sixth Avenue and West 45th Street when someone repeatedly pushed into him from behind. He then felt a painful sting in his right forearm, according to the complaint. The man turned around and saw a woman matching the first victim’s description. He told investigators she threatened him in Russian, warning that she had a gun and would shoot him if he did not leave. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT She allegedly reached toward the inside of her jacket, leading him to believe she had a firearm. Police said the 37-year-old suffered a cut to his forearm and declined medical attention at the scene. He also told investigators he saw the woman approach another man nearby and ask in English whether he was Jewish. When the man said he was Muslim, she apologized and walked away, according to the complaint. The complaint’s timeline places the attacks five minutes apart. The initial NYPD statement listed police response times two hours apart. WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE A Hate Crimes Task Force detective reviewed surveillance video from West 47th Street and created a still image of the suspect. Another NYPD officer recognized Mochalova based on previous interactions with her, according to the complaint. Mochalova was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault as a hate crime, one count of second-degree menacing as a hate crime, and two counts each of fourth-degree criminal possession of a weapon and second-degree aggravated harassment, the DA’s office confirmed. The judge set bail at $50,000 cash or $150,000 bond, half the amounts prosecutors requested. Her next court appearance is Oct. 29. Her attorney, Legal Aid’s Lila Carpenter, questioned whether police had identified the right person during Sunday’s arraignment, the New York Post reported. "These allegations are concerning. Whether they’re my client’s is a different story," Carpenter told the court, according to the outlet. The Post identified the 26-year-old victim as a rabbi and reported that the attacker used a syringe. Neither the police statement to Fox News Digital nor the complaint identified the sharp object as a syringe. The rabbi told the Post he believed his appearance made him a target. Despite the attack, he returned to the area the next day to continue Jewish outreach, crediting his grandparents, who survived the Holocaust, with inspiring him. MAMDANI PLEDGES MILLIONS TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM WHILE LEAVING KEY QUESTION UNRESOLVED Advocacy group StopAntisemitism also condemned the reported attack. "What has happened to NYC, a once safe haven for Jews?" the group wrote on X. The attacks come as confirmed hate crimes across New York City rose nearly 13% during the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to NYPD figures. Anti-Jewish incidents accounted for more than half of the city’s 463 confirmed hate crimes. Police recorded 245 anti-Jewish hate crimes through September, up from 242 during the same period in 2025. articles.title: Serbia’s strongman leader Vucic concedes defeat to student-led movement in seismic political shift
articles.summary: The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.
articles.body: The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government. It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led for 14 years. High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country. Serbia’s 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students’ List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105. “The Students’ List has won,” Vucic told supporters at his party’s election-night event, though he blamed Serbia’s independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an “American deep state” for the loss. Belgrade erupts in celebration Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students’ List, which he said took around 2.2 million. Supporters of the Students’ List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting: “Aleksandar is gone,” referring to Vucic. The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day. Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic’s loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city. Protests over corruption lead to Vucic’s fall Vucic was seeking to become Serbia’s prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign. Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station. Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia’s voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties — the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media. Student movement While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia’s fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office. The newly formed Students’ List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. This approach was meant to counter Vucic’s one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students’ message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy. The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas — Vucic’s traditional strongholds. The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests. The vote was closely watched in the EU Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70%, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time. Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday’s vote in a candidate nation for the bloc’s membership. Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying. Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists. Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

articles.title: Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power
articles.summary: National Rally’s Le Pen launches presidential campaign against backdrop of protests and social, economic discontent.
articles.body:
Orleans, France – Marine Le Pen took to the stage with a clear message: She would lead France’s “renaissance” as the country sank into crisis – and she would do so soon.

The far-right figure’s words were met with cheers from thousands of supporters gathered in Orleans in central France on Sunday, as she launched her presidential campaign against a backdrop of mass demonstrations and widespread social and economic discontent.

“Marine présidente!” the crowd chanted, waving French flags beneath a sea of red and blue lights. Organisers said 8,500 supporters had gathered in a venue transformed into a fort for the event.

Standing tall on stage in a pink blazer, her hair impeccably coiffed, Le Pen spoke with the confidence of a leader who believes the presidency is within reach.

Riding high in the polls, with candidates from the right, left and centre trailing behind her, she presented the election as a historic opportunity to restore France’s past glory.

“This is a story to be written, a destiny to be fulfilled,” she told the crowd, which erupted in cheers.

Her pitch was a promise to restore authority and security in a country she portrayed as having lost control.

“We are going to re-establish the rule of law,” she said, drawing loud applause from supporters wearing “Marine présidente” T-shirts.

Manon Funeau, 21, a business school student, was among the supporters.

“What they propose are values that resonate with me, that vibrate within me,” she said. “Honestly, I feel at home here.”

Le Pen’s speech comes as the country is at a crossroads. France has been shaken by a wave of protests since mid-September, a movement sparked by high school students in a Paris suburb that grew into a nationwide mobilisation tapping into widespread discontent.

Over the past two weekends, largely peaceful protests have been accompanied by episodes of violence on a scale rarely seen in recent years.

On October 17 , shops were looted and ransacked, and more than 2,000 people were arrested as hundreds of thousands took to the streets of French cities. A similar dynamic unfolded the following weekend , though on a smaller scale. The protests show little sign of abating, with calls for further demonstrations already circulating.

The unrest has given Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) an opportunity to play one of its favourite cards: presenting itself as the guarantor of law and order. It has fuelled criticism of President Emmanuel Macron over his handling of public security, allowing Le Pen to accuse him of incompetence and the far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon – a contender in the coming elections – of encouraging the violence.

“I believe that my country is currently drifting off course,” said Nadede, a 56-year-old who began voting for RN in 2024 over what she said was the country’s growing lack of security. She did not spell out any specific event.

“I think that the only person capable of setting it back on the right track is Marine Le Pen – especially since, up until now, everyone else who has run for office has struggled to do so,” she said.

Outside the convention hall, the scale of the security operation offered a glimpse of the tensions surrounding the event. Police checks began at departure stations in Paris and continued on arrival, while officers in full gear moved through train carriages during the journey.

Orleans itself had been brought to a near standstill. All businesses were shut and public transport suspended.

Standing almost alone in the city’s main square was the statue of Joan of Arc, surrounded only by fences. A day earlier, about 3,000 police officers had been deployed to prevent unrest as anti-RN protesters gathered against what they say is a xenophobic and racist party.

Orleans was no casual choice. For a party that has long sought to cast itself as the guardian of French identity and national sovereignty, the city is inseparable from the story of Joan of Arc, the 15th-century heroine who helped lift the English siege of Orléans in 1429 and became a symbol of France’s resistance and liberation.

For decades, the far right has claimed her as an emblem of national pride, invoking the image of a warrior who came to save France from foreign domination. Le Pen herself has drawn parallels between Joan’s mission and her political ambitions.

The crowd at the RN Congress offered a glimpse of how the party has expanded its appeal to a wider section of society: from young people from urban centres to middle-class workers who used to vote for the centrist party.

Only a few years ago, the party was still considered on the fringes of French politics. Its growth has been driven in part by a carefully crafted strategy known as dédiabolisation , or de-demonisation, developed over the past two decades to broaden the party’s base while tempering its rhetoric and distancing it from positions that had made it toxic to many voters.

The party has long been associated with racism, xenophobia and anti-Semitism. Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was convicted of hate speech, including for describing Nazi gas chambers as “a detail of history”. He was expelled from the party in 2015.

Marine Le Pen has sought to broaden RN’s appeal, combining restrictive immigration policies with promises of social protection. The party has gained ground in working-class areas traditionally associated with the left, including former Communist strongholds, by presenting itself as a defender of public services and the purchasing power of everyday people.

While RN has long abandoned some of its most radical proposals, including leaving the Eurozone and pursuing a fully fledged “Frexit”, the election of such a eurosceptic to the helm of the European Union’s second-largest economy would send shockwaves. She has pledged a referendum to challenge the primacy of EU law over migration policy, as well as an annual 11-billion-euro ($12.3bn) reduction in France’s contribution to the bloc.

The party’s membership has nearly tripled, with approximately 112,000 members now paying their dues, up from fewer than 37,000 in 2022.

“The party has been gaining ground at every level: mayors, deputies, senators. Usually, when a movement seems on the rise, people join,” said Baptiste Roger-Lacan, a historian and political analyst with a focus on far-right parties in Europe. “It also shows how it is less and less socially damaging to be a member of the RN.”

But the party’s programme “is still fraught with fiscal absurdity”, Roger-Lacan said. “They still want to implement racist laws, which are bound to provoke widespread anger, and their diplomatic agenda is still pro-Russian and anti-EU – even if they don’t advocate Frexit any more.”

Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s second-in-command and Le Pen protégé – an impeccably dressed 31-year-old who looks like a cross between the Wolf of Wall Street and Superman’s alter ego, Clark Kent – also spoke at the event.

“No one should be intimidated by their political opinions,” he said, speaking ahead of his mentor.

Some observers say the October 17 protests and their aftermath have proved a gift to RN, allowing the party to not only reinforce its law-and-order message but also to shift attention away from recent difficulties.

In September, investigative outlet Mediapart published allegations that Bardella had expressed anti-Semitic views in private messages dating back to his teenage years. He denied the allegations and announced legal action against the journalists.

The episode posed a challenge for a party that has spent years trying to shed its xenophobic image and recast itself as a supporter of Israel.

Bardella has also reportedly differed with Le Pen over the party’s economic agenda and whether to make her proposed ban on the wearing of the Islamic headscarf in public spaces a central campaign issue.

Yet, at the Congress, those tensions appeared to have been set aside, at least publicly.

“Marine president – a Bardella government” was the slogan, projecting unity as Le Pen launched her presidential bid and Bardella positioned himself as her prospective head of government.

articles.title: Grange Hospital deemed 'dangerous' online but staff call it safest in Wales
articles.summary: Grange University Hospital has faced criticism over long delays, overcrowding and staff shortages.
articles.body:
Senior staff at Wales' newest hospital insist it's safe - despite claims that it is dangerous and failing.

Since it opened early in the pandemic, Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen, has been under fire over concerns about long delays, overcrowding, staff shortages and the quality of its care.

Criticism has been especially intense on social media, with some in the comments even urging people to stay away.

Bosses admit staff feel "devastated" that patient confidence could be dented but insist the hospital performs better than many others on patient safety, including survival rates.

They are urging those who are seriously unwell not to be afraid to seek help.

As dawn breaks over Cwmbran on a clear autumn day the mist in the valley lifts, revealing sunlit hills and the imposing sight of the hospital - the serene picture is in stark contrast to what's happening inside.

The PA announcement in A&E is clear - somebody's life is in danger and they'll soon be arriving by ambulance.

But all eight beds at the Emergency Department's (ED) resuscitation unit, where the sickest patients go, are already full.

Staff have to decide quickly which patient to move.

But two similar "crash calls" have already come in by ambulance, as well as someone who walked into an already-full reception having a suspected heart attack.

Overall there are more than 90 patients in the department with the longest wait about 18 hours.

"We're currently over capacity," says Dr Zoe Morgan-Pittard, who is so busy that she's placed stickers on her arms to remind her who she's been assessing.

"We've had to move three patients already who probably aren't well enough.

"But the sickest patients have to take priority - we're having to make fluid decisions.

"We're putting patients in any extra space we can find... but there's a lot of block and very little flow.

"Everybody is working hard, but unfortunately the hospital isn't big enough."

One of those extra spaces is located behind some cubicles at the back of the A&E.

Margaret Giles, 84, from nearby Croesyceiliog, has spent the past nine hours on a trolley there, after slipping and injuring her hip.

"It's not satisfactory – but needs must," she says.

"I went to see the lady at the desk [during the night] because she wanted to go to the toilet… and [the lady] said 'can't she walk to the toilet?' I said 'no! It's a suspected broken hip'."

There is relief when X-rays show Margaret's hip isn't broken, and soon she'll be able to go home.

Staff tell us there are strict criteria meaning only the least sick patients can be kept in these open spaces - but it's an experience both Margaret and Alan don't want to repeat.

"We've never been in here before," Alan gestures , "it's the first time for me - and hope it's the last."

"I don't think it's the staff, it's the system."

One reason people are treated in open spaces is to free up the ambulances arriving outside - we counted at least eight waiting outside during our visit.

But previously crews could expect to spend an entire 12-hour shift waiting to hand over patients. Now the target is to release them within 45 minutes.

On the day of our visit, due to the pressures, 33% of the ambulances were released within 45 minutes, but it was 67% for the previous 30 days - a huge improvement compared to before.

"We've seen a vast improvement," Darren Panniers of the Welsh Ambulance Service says.

"We are responding to patients quicker in the community, particularly around calls which involve stroke and heart attacks."

But the efforts to release ambulances also involves improving the flow of patients through and out of the entire hospital.

Surgical teams now go to A&E to spot the patients they can treat more quickly while urgent patients needing same-day care can go to different department.

But for years, the biggest logjam has been delays in releasing patients who have completed treatment.

So at the Grange they have built a portacabin, with 10 beds and 15 chairs where patients can prepare to go home or move to another hospital and staff can, wash, feed and care for them, as if on a ward.

They also liaise with families and social services to try to speed up discharge.

"It allows us to free up beds quickly and it's somewhere quieter more comfortable for patients to wait," senior nurse Sian Williams tells us.

"I always say even one bed makes all the difference to the ambulances outside."

Yet despite these and other efforts the Grange, since it opened early due to Covid in September 2020, has been under intense scrutiny .

The £350m "super hospital" was based on a model where lots of specialist care including intensive, surgery and A&E were centralised from existing hospitals in Newport and Abergavenny.

The assumption was that community services would be strong enough to take up the slack.

One of the health boards top bosses, chief operating officer Leanne Watkins, says: "Bringing our teams together - for example, in paediatrics and obs and gynae we had very fragile services spread across the system, and when you think of the risk that are contained in maternity services, for example, in paediatrics, that's enormous.

"So, I think we would have really struggled without [the Grange].

"I think we could have benefited from some additional beds."

Despite this, the health board remains in level four measures - the second highest level of Welsh government oversight, due to worries linked to urgent and emergency care.

And social media posts go further, dubbing the Grange as "dangerous", "awful" and "a disgrace".

"I don't believe that [those criticisms] are fair," Watkins says.

"We have amongst the best mortality rates in Wales, and in fact, for some procedures, things like fractured neck or femur (hip) and emergency surgery, we we rate right up there with the best in the UK.

"If you're unwell, critically unwell, it is a great place to be."

She said the criticisms are driven by a small number of complaints, and reduce public confidence.

"For our staff, it is devastating to read what's been said.

"We know we need to do better, we know delays are unacceptable, but the teams work incredibly hard, and I'm for one proud of them.

The health board's own data suggests death rates at the hospital are lower than similar hospitals in Wales, taking into account the nature of the population and the severity of cases.

Figures also suggest the proportion of patients who die in the Grange's emergency department remains below the Welsh average and has shown sustained improvement.

"I just encourage people to look at the facts. I know sometimes it's really hard, especially on social media that people can get messages that can make them feel low in confidence [but] please come and talk to us," Dr Seema Srivastava says.

"It makes me sad," deputy head of nursing Lorna Lear says.

"Obviously, sometimes there are instances where the care is less than what we expect.

"But we always listen to the feedback... and we always want to improve our services and give our patients the best possible care."

"So when we do see those negative headlines, it can be quite upsetting."

"If you have been waiting excessive hours to be seen, you're going to be frustrated and that's okay. It's understandable," consultant and director of urgent care Owain Chandler adds.

After a seven-hour tour of the hospital we're back at A&E, where staff have seen 274 patients during the course of the day.

The nurse in charge, Sam Taylor-Harley, says: "We've had some more heart attacks, myocardial infarctions, we've had a couple of trauma calls, we've had a couple of admissions to the ITU upstairs, and we've also had some infection prevention control issues coming in as well."

As we prepare to leave the hospital, a patient with life-threatening wounds is rushed in by air ambulance medics.

More than a dozen staff from all parts of the hospital are ready and waiting.

If you're as seriously ill as this - you'll never have to wait to be seen, but that means less serious cases are likely to wait even longer.

The Welsh government said NHS staff are "working incredibly hard" to give patients compassionate care, and early plans are in place to help with a challenging winter.

It said Aneurin Bevan health board, which runs the Grange hospital, still needs to improve adding:

"(It) is currently in Level 4 escalation for urgent and emergency care performance (and) must show clear improvement plans, better unscheduled care performance, a stronger grip on urgent and emergency care concerns, and clearer information for patients on how to access care."

articles.title: Rogers fires back at Welker over El-Sayed's Muslim Brotherhood controversy, 'You are giving him a pass'
articles.summary: Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers accused NBC's Kristen Welker of defending his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed during a heated "Meet the Press" exchange.
articles.body: Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers fired back at NBC's "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker on Sunday over his allegations about Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, accusing Welker of defending his rival during a heated exchange about the Islamist organization. Rogers challenged Welker after she said that El-Sayed had already disavowed any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and defended her previous interview with El-Sayed in which he denied any ties to the group. "No, he has not, he dismissed the question ... I don't know why you give this guy a pass," Rogers said, as the two interrupted each other. "You are giving him a pass on something he should be accountable for." MIKE ROGERS PRESSES CNN'S DANA BASH ON WHY THE PRESS IS 'EAGER' TO DEFEND ABDUL EL-SAYED Welker pressed Rogers on his own 2012 remarks, displaying a past quote where he said the U.S. would have to "reach out to and talk to" moderate members of the Muslim Brotherhood and asking whether he acknowledged having once been willing to engage with them. Rogers accused Welker of twisting his words to defend El-Sayed rather than scrutinize his opponent's record. He explained that, as House Intelligence Committee chairman at the time, his focus was on preserving intelligence cooperation between Egypt and Israel to prevent further regional violence. "What you're doing now is trying to twist this thing to defend your position for letting him lie to you," he added. The confrontation intensified when Welker pressed Rogers about President Donald Trump's characterization of El-Sayed as a violent terrorist. Welker challenged the accusation, saying there was no evidence to support it. She also noted that El-Sayed had denied any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood and publicly disavowed the organization. Rogers rejected the suggestion that he had personally described his Democratic opponent as a terrorist. "I've never called him a terrorist," Rogers said. MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED Rogers' campaign doubled down on his criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, with spokesperson Abby Ronson questioning El-Sayed's responses and urging national media outlets to scrutinize his record. "Abdul is an Oxford-trained debater," Ronson said. "Yet every time he’s asked about his support of the Muslim Brotherhood, he deflects, gets angry and dismisses the question. Michiganders deserve an answer on what should be an incredibly easy question to answer." "Why won’t his campaign put out an equivocal [sic] statement disavowing a terrorist organization? The national media should start asking him why that is instead of making excuses for him," she continued. Rogers' allegations stem from previously reported connections between El-Sayed, members of his family and the Muslim Brotherhood, including a 2012 letter supporting Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood-backed president, Mohamed Morsi. The Washington Free Beacon reported that El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian American community figures who signed a November 2012 letter backing Morsi's decisions and urging him to purge Egypt's police and media. The outlet identified El-Sayed as a signatory to the letter, which was published as Morsi faced criticism for expanding his presidential powers. OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Past social media posts from El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, recently surfaced and described their family's history with the Muslim Brotherhood. In one 2012 post, Abdelhadi acknowledged longstanding family connections to the organization. "My family has long been MB, but I've always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively," Abdelhadi said. In another post, Abdelhadi described a conversation with her mother about participating in Muslim Brotherhood activism while attending college in Egypt during the 1970s. El-Sayed has maintained that he was raised by his father and stepmother and has accused Rogers of exploiting his Muslim faith for political purposes. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed for comment, but did not immediately receive a response. He denied that he or his family had ties to the organization when Welker questioned him during an Oct. 11 appearance on "Meet the Press." articles.title: Obama campaigns for Democrats, and France demonstrations continue: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama, appearing in Ohio Saturday at his first campaign rally for the midterm elections, characterized President Donald Trump as an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama, appearing in Ohio on Saturday at his first campaign rally of this fall’s midterm elections, called President Donald Trump an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises. Obama’s visit was aimed at boosting two Democrats: Amy Acton, the party’s nominee for governor; and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has mounted a comeback bid for his old job. Obama was particularly scornful of Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad aimed at Acton, saying there is “no line” Ramaswamy won’t cross. Later in the night, Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit. The city, where 75% of the population is Black, is crucial to statewide victories. Notable quote Obama made pointed criticisms of his Republican successor, lambasting Trump for his focus on White House ballroom construction. Iranian plots to kill U.S. officials have reached ‘advanced stages,’ intel memo warns Iran has stepped up efforts to target U.S. personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, according to a memo Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday. The memo warned that “the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages.” A U.S. official confirmed the memo’s authenticity to NBC News after it was first reported by Axios. The intelligence comes days after sources told NBC News that the U.S. military has been quietly scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East. The State Department has also ordered further staff reductions at multiple diplomatic posts in the region, including in Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Jordan, according to a State Department official. Clayton told Rubio that the risk was “relevant to more individuals than are currently cleared to receive this information,” adding: “We will make every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so you can share it with State Department personnel at your discretion.” ‘Meet the Press’ Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should testify before the Senate on the Starlink satellite limitations that disrupted Ukrainian military operations. If Democrats retake the Senate, Schiff told moderator Kristen Welker, “Defense Secretary Hegseth should be brought in. Anyone who has knowledge of what happened.” Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers responded to Trump calling Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a “violent terrorist.” “I’ve never called [El-Sayed] a terrorist,” Rogers said on “Meet the Press” after being asked about Trump’s comments. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a woman as president. “Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I’ve heard everyone say, ‘You can’t have this person or that person,’” the governor told “Meet the Press.” Politics in brief Drop the stop: Democrats urged a federal judge to dismiss the Trump administration’s challenge to Alaska’s Senate race.Early voting: Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.Analysis: How Democrats could win the House, how the GOP could hang on, and where to look for a wave. Mass protests challenge Macron as French police use tear gas and water cannons More than 100,000 people marched in Paris on Saturday over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging President Emmanuel Macron’s government in a largely peaceful demonstration before clashes broke out near the march’s end point. Students, union members, environmentalists and other groups marched through cold, rainy weather. Near the march’s end point, some demonstrators threw bottles and rocks at police, who then charged at the crowd, fired tear gas and used water cannons. NBC News witnessed no looting. “We are mostly students,” one person told NBC News, referencing the protests. “We’re not here to break things. We’re not here to mess with the cops or anyone. We’re just here to protest.” 12 injured in shooting near Florida A&M University stadium Twelve people, including several minors, were injured in a shooting near Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium, where homecoming celebrations included a football game Saturday. The Tallahassee Police Department said in a statement that 11 of the 12 were shot and that three victims had serious injuries. Six of the injured are under 18 years old, the department said. Tallahassee police said a fight may have preceded the gunfire. No arrests have been reported. “Early findings indicate a physical altercation occurred prior to the shooting,” the department said. Inside the controversial call that ended Game 2 of the World Series The Milwaukee Brewers are two wins away from the first World Series title in franchise history, and they got a little help from an incredibly close call Saturday night. With the Brewers leading 5-4 in the top of the ninth, the Rays had a runner on third with two outs and designated hitter Yandy Díaz at the plate. On a 3-2 pitch that would have been Ball 4, Díaz tried to check his swing on a curveball from Aaron Ashby. Home plate umpire Jim Wolf initially ruled that Díaz hadn’t swung, which would have sent him to first base. But Milwaukee catcher William Contreras appealed to the first base umpire, who ruled that Díaz had gone around. The strikeout ended the game. More sports news: WNBA: Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries scored 17 points and led a stellar defensive effort to beat the Atlanta Dream 67-62 on Saturday, evening up the WNBA Finals 2-2. NFL: American football fans visiting France for the Saints-Steelers game told NBC News their trips were mostly unaffected by demonstrations, giving Parisians a rare compliment for their welcoming demeanor. In case you missed it Brazilians vote Sunday in a tight runoff between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.Elon Musk acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, imposed restrictions on the use of its Starlink satellite system in Ukraine last week. Ukraine said Saturday that Starlink and its military variant, Starshield, were both fully functional again after a prolonged outage.Hundreds of homes remained evacuated and without electricity Saturday after days of heavy rain surged water from the Colorado mountains into the New Mexico and Arizona desert.Six Flags said it will add seat belts to a roller coaster from which a man was ejected and fell to his death earlier this month. The suspect in the fatal freeway shooting of a high school girl just outside St. Louis is being investigated in connection with a second roadway shooting, federal court documents show.

articles.title: In 1973, the Philadelphia Orchestra became the first US orchestra to perform in China; ahead of its 14th China tour, former ambassador David Cohen and his wife pledged $10.5 million to support global tours and new music
articles.summary: Music has crossed political borders for decades, and the Philadelphia Orchestra is preparing to continue that tradition with a $10.5 million gift from
articles.body: Music has crossed political borders for decades, and the Philadelphia Orchestra is preparing to continue that tradition with a $10.5 million gift from former US ambassador David L Cohen and his wife, Rhonda R Cohen. According to the orchestra and Ensemble Arts’ official announcement on October 22, 2026, the commitment will support international tours, cultural exchanges and new music. It comes ahead of the orchestra’s 14th visit to China, continuing a relationship that began in 1973, when it became the first American orchestra to perform in the People’s Republic of China. The gift will also support emerging composers and strengthen the organisation’s leadership.$10.5 million gift to support cultural diplomacyThe commitment is designed to strengthen the Philadelphia Orchestra’s role as a cultural ambassador through performances and exchanges across national borders. According to the official announcement, the gift will establish the Fund for Cultural Diplomacy, supporting domestic and international tours, residencies, concerts, recordings and educational exchanges.The initiative aims to use music to build relationships between communities and countries, even when diplomatic and political relations face challenges. David Cohen and Rhonda Cohen said they had witnessed how music could build trust and bring people together during their years of public service. The announcement comes as the orchestra prepares to travel to South Korea and China. Its forthcoming Asian tour will combine performances with opportunities for cultural exchange, including engagement with local communities and arts leaders. The funding is intended to help sustain such activities over the longer term.From a historic China visit to a continuing diplomatic roleThe Philadelphia Orchestra’s relationship with China dates back to 1973, when it became the first American orchestra to perform in the country. More than five decades later, its upcoming visit will be its 14th tour of China, the highest number of such visits by any American orchestra, according to the organisation.The orchestra’s international work has also included performances in Canada. During Cohen’s tenure as US ambassador to Canada from 2021 to 2025, the ensemble toured Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa. In an interview with WHYY, David L Cohen described the goodwill and attention generated by the orchestra’s performances. The experience reinforced his belief that cultural institutions can contribute to international relations in ways that traditional diplomatic engagements may not always achieve.The upcoming tour will open in Incheon, South Korea, on November 5, before continuing to Seoul and then China, where the orchestra is scheduled to perform in Haikou and Beijing, with additional residency activities in Shenzhen and Shanghai. The visit will bring together music, international engagement and opportunities to strengthen cultural connections.New fund to champion underrepresented composersAlongside international touring, the donation will support artistic innovation through the creation of the Artistic Innovation and Discovery Fund. Guided by music and artistic director Yannick Nézet-Séguin’s artistic vision, the fund will help the orchestra perform works by overlooked, underrepresented and emerging composers, while also celebrating the contributions of Jewish artists.The initiative aligns with Nézet-Séguin’s efforts to broaden the classical repertoire beyond its established composers. The orchestra has previously championed works by Black American composers Florence Price and William Grant Still. Its recording of Price’s music won a Grammy Award in 2022, bringing renewed attention to a composer whose work had long received less prominence in the classical music world.The new fund is intended to build on such efforts by creating more opportunities for diverse artistic voices to reach audiences through performances and recordings. It will help the orchestra expand its repertoire and bring a wider range of musical perspectives to the concert hall.Leadership position to carry the Cohens’ namesThe $10.5 million commitment will also provide an endowment for the organisation’s top executive position. Ryan Fleur, president and CEO of The Philadelphia Orchestra and Ensemble Arts, will hold the newly named ‘Ambassador David L Cohen and Rhonda R Cohen President and CEO’ position.The naming recognises the couple’s contribution to the institution and their involvement in civic and philanthropic life in Philadelphia. David Cohen previously served as senior adviser to the CEO and senior executive vice-president at Comcast NBCUniversal, and as US ambassador to Canada. Rhonda Cohen is a retired attorney and civic leader who chairs the board of the Glenmede Trust Company and has served on several educational and community organisations.The gift was announced following a major fundraising campaign by the Philadelphia Orchestra and Ensemble Arts that raised $344 million, surpassing its original target of $330 million. The organisation said the campaign proceeds would support operations, maintain venues including the Kimmel Center, Academy of Music and Miller Theater, and strengthen its endowment.Music as a bridge between countriesThe donation comes as the orchestra prepares to return to Asia at a time of international political uncertainty. Its leadership has emphasised that the tour is centred on music, cultural exchange and opportunities to build connections across borders.By combining international performances with educational activities, support for new music and long-term institutional funding, the Cohen gift is intended to extend the orchestra’s work beyond the concert hall. Its historic China tours have helped establish a distinctive role for the ensemble in cultural diplomacy, while the new funds aim to sustain that role for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Southwest Airlines is launching 11 new nonstop international routes from Las Vegas, Nashville, Austin, Columbus and Pittsburgh starting November.
articles.body: Southwest Airlines will add 11 new nonstop international routes to its schedule beginning in November, giving travelers more options for their next tropical escape. On Nov. 1, the carrier will start offering nonstop service from Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas to Puerto Vallarta (PVR), the New York Post reported. Southwest Airlines already has command of more than 40% of all flight operations at LAS. SOUTHWEST CAPTAIN ADMITS HIS 'LIP WAS QUIVERING' DURING CO-PILOT DAUGHTER'S SURPRISE SPEECH ON FINAL FLIGHT In February 2027, the airline will begin offering nonstop flights from Nashville International Airport (BNA) to Liberia, and to Aruba (AUA) in March. Additionally, all Americans wishing to go to Liberia must procure a visa before they visit, no matter the length of their trip, according to the U.S. Department of State. Southwest Airlines will be the only carrier with direct flights for all four of the Nashville routes. Southwest will add four new international routes from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) in June, as well. Flights will go to San José, Costa Rica, beginning in March, and there will be service to Liberia, Punta Cana and Nassau starting in June. articles.title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
articles.summary: Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July.
articles.body:
Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.

Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.

On the eve of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The BBC understands the government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas and/or they will be offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.

Some people may choose not to accept accommodation, but ministers say support will still be offered to them.

The government said initial funding had seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.

Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.

Ahead of hosting the summit, Burnham said: "Rough sleeping isn't a fact of life. It's a thing governments either choose to accept or don't.

"Well I don't accept it. That's why we're doubling funding so that people aren't just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this Parliament too.

"But we can't do it alone. If we're going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we're bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts."

More than 30 organisations have pledged support for the plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities.

Meanwhile, the National Housing Federation is working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.

However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.

The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.

Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.

It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.

Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.

The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."

The Bed Every Night scheme Burnham set up while mayor in the region now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.

He pledged to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester by 2020 when he came into power.

When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.

The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021 but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.

Across England, government figures show the number of people sleeping rough is at its highest level since records began in 2010.

Lam continued: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.

"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.

"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Around 35 to 40 shops were completely gutted after a massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station, in the early hours
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Around 35 to 40 shops were completely gutted after a massive fire broke out at Shiv Market, opposite Jammu Railway Station, in the early hours of Monday. No casualties or injuries have been reported so far, while fire and emergency services teams were working to bring the blaze under control. The cause of the fire remains unknown.BJP MLA Vikram Randhawa said the fire reportedly began due to a short circuit in one shop before spreading rapidly to adjoining establishments. Shiv Market is a major commercial hub with shops selling dry fruits and blankets, as well as eateries and dhabas.“The fire started with a short circuit in one shop and spread rapidly, engulfing surrounding shops. By the time the fire brigade arrived, the entire market had been consumed by the flames. In my estimation, about 35 to 40 shops have been completely gutted,” Randhawa said.Describing the firefighting efforts, the MLA said the blaze had engulfed the entire market by the time the situation could be brought under control. He added that police personnel and senior officers were actively involved in managing the situation.“As it kept growing, by the time the whole system came under control, it had already engulfed the entire market. Right now, our police are completely alert and actively controlling the situation. You can see that from the SHO to our SP, everyone is personally involved, even holding and dragging pipes all the way to the shops,” Randhawa said.A shopkeeper said at least 25 to 30 shops had suffered total losses and urged the administration to provide compensation to those affected.“The entire market has been reduced to ashes. At least 25 to 30 shops are a total loss. We pray to God to grant everyone the strength to cope with this — the loss is immense, a total loss. I also urge the administration to step in as quickly as possible and ensure that compensation is provided without delay,” the shopkeeper said.Randhawa said the full extent of the damage could be assessed only after the situation was completely under control. He said shopkeepers were cooperating with the administration, with the deputy commissioner, SP South, DSP, SHO and their teams present at the site. articles.title: Bulgaria election heads to a run-off amid low voter turnout
articles.summary: Bulgarians will now choose between President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov next week.
articles.body:
Bulgaria’s presidential election is heading to a run-off after polls closed with low voter turnout and no candidate passing the required threshold.

Incumbent President Iliana Iotova received between 35 and 36.5 percent of votes on Sunday , according to exit polls. She will now face former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who scored between 31 and 33.5 percent, in a second round on November 1.

Minister of Interior Ivan Demerdzhiev said the elections “took place peacefully, without the usual practices of vote buying and vote manipulation”, Bulgarian National Television reported.

The NATO and European Union member state saw 27 presidential candidates run in the election.

A run-off was expected, as turnout must reach more than 50 percent of registered voters, and the candidate must secure more than 50 percent of the votes to win in the first round.

Voter turnout was 22.2 percent as of 8pm local time (18:00 GMT), according to the Measure polling agency.

Rising energy costs, inflation, attacks in the Black Sea and Russia’s war in Ukraine were the major issues in the lead-up to the vote.

A series of drone strikes on ships off Bulgaria’s coast, condemned by both candidates, dominated headlines during the campaign period.

Leftist Iotova is backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whose Progressive Bulgaria party enjoyed success in April’s parliamentary elections. Iotova became president in January after serving as vice president.

A former member of the European Parliament and a journalist, she ran as an independent with the backing of both Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party.

Should she win, she is expected to keep Bulgaria in line with Europe, while calling for improved relations with Russia.

After casting her vote, Yotova said she wanted to address “the dire issue of poverty” in Bulgaria, as well as “inequalities and regional disputes”, the AFP news agency reported.

“I believe that there must be peace, stability, and security,” she added.

Gyurov has the support of the country’s pro-Western opposition and signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine as prime minister.

He said on Sunday that he wanted “a Bulgaria that looks forward, a country that is European, free, and proud”.

“Next week, Bulgaria must choose between two personalities, two directions,” he said after the vote, and invited Iotova to a debate before the next round.

Although the role of president is largely ceremonial, the president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation and sign treaties.

articles.title: Presidential race in Bulgaria heads to runoff due to record low turnout
articles.summary: The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff, according to election officials.
articles.body: The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff, according to election officials. A record low turnout, attributed by observers to a general mistrust in politicians resulting in voter apathy, will pit two contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarized contest on Nov. 1. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-Western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova, setting clear lines of division regarding the country’s future relationships with other nations. Bulgarians voted against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The vote is the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev after its triumph in parliamentary elections in April. Despite a record number of candidates, the race had been expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent Yotova, backed by Radev’s party, and former caretaker Prime Minister Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties. The campaign focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country. The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict and prompted the government to ask Bulgaria’s partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security. Candidates also sought to address public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet. The election had been expected to go to a runoff as none of the 27 candidates was expected to win outright. Turnout must be above 50% of 6.6 million registered voters, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Bulgaria’s incumbent president is a front-runner Yotova, a 62-year-old journalist and former member of the European Parliament, is the country’s incumbent president and a front-runner in the race. She previously served as vice president under Radev, during his two terms as head of state. She took over the presidency in January 2026, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now seeking her own mandate. She’s running as an independent but also has the official backing of Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party, where her career began. If she wins, Yotova will become Bulgaria’s first elected female president. Analysts expect her to continue Radev’s policy to keep Bulgaria on its European path but at the same time call for improved relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine. Addressing supporters at a rally this week, Yotova said she “advocated for peace through negotiations, rather than force.” Observers say that Yotova’s victory would keep the presidency in the hands of the ruling majority, and such concentration of power could prevent institutions maintaining effective checks and balances on policy decisions. A former deputy central bank governor is the main challenger in the race Yotova’s main challenger is economist Andrei Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister who led the country in the early months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition. Gyurov, who has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership. “I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position,” he told supporters this week. Latest opinion polls give Yotova an edge in the first round of the race by giving her between 40 percent and 45 percent, versus Gyurov’s 25-30 %, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. But some observers believe that Gyurov could have a better chance in a runoff, where results can be influenced by voters who supported candidates eliminated in the first round. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. While the post is primarily ceremonial, the direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

articles.summary: Video shows a stolen car slamming into a South Carolina home before two teenagers fled, prompting Greenville County deputies to deploy K9s and a drone.
articles.body: A stolen car barreled through neighborhood yards and smashed into a South Carolina home before two teenagers ran, triggering a search involving deputies, K9 teams and a drone, authorities said. Video released by the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office shows the car slamming into the house before deputies rush toward the wreck and chase a fleeing suspect. "Is everybody alright?" a deputy can be heard asking as authorities check the home for anyone who might be hurt. FOUR TEENS KILL COUPLE IN HEAD-ON CRASH AFTER STEALING G-WAGON, LEADING COPS ON HOURS-LONG CHASE: POLICE The sheriff’s office said deputies attempted to stop the reported stolen vehicle around 2:30 p.m. Oct. 15. The driver fled, but deputies said they did not pursue the car before it crashed into the home on Renwood Road in Simpsonville. Two teenagers, ages 15 and 16, were eventually arrested and charged with possession of a stolen vehicle, authorities said. No injuries were reported. WATCH: DEPUTIES HUNT WANTED MAN THROUGH CORNFIELD AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE CAUGHT ON CAMERA The video shows one deputy running after a fleeing suspect while another heads toward the damaged home. The passenger was quickly taken into custody, while the search for the driver brought help from above and on the ground. K9 teams used multiple dogs to track the driver’s path, and drone operators provided an aerial view of the neighborhood, according to the sheriff’s office. The video also shows a dog picking up a scent collected from the vehicle before tracking the driver. BLOODHOUND K-9 UNIT HELPS BRING GEORGIA MANHUNT TO END WITH ARREST OF SUSPECT ACCUSED OF SHOOTING WOMAN "When someone decides to run from law enforcement in Greenville County, they quickly learn that our deputies have more than one way to find them," the sheriff’s office wrote in a post accompanying the video. "You can run, but our deputies have a pretty impressive toolbox. And they know how to use it," the agency added. For neighbors, the crash brought a frightening interruption to an otherwise routine afternoon. "I was just putting my baby down for a nap, and I heard a big crash outside," next-door neighbor Rachel Bush told WYFF. Just minutes earlier, Bush said, she had been walking outside with her baby and dog. "We were grateful we were back inside before everything happened," she told the outlet. DRIVER RELEASED WITHOUT CHARGES AFTER PICKUP KILLS BOY, 6, AND MAN ON KANSAS SOCCER FIELD One of the home’s residents told WYFF that no one was home when the car crashed through the front door. He and his fiancé returned from an errand minutes later to find the damage. The resident said the car missed another vehicle in the garage by inches, leaving behind an extensive cleanup and repair job. Another neighbor, Robert Belcher, told WYFF he offered support after seeing what happened. "I don’t know what to say to you but thank God no one was at home," Belcher recalled telling his neighbor. articles.title: No risk of ammonia contamination, officials say, after fire at Oregon seafood plant prompted evacuations
articles.summary: There was no further threat of ammonia contamination, officials said Sunday afternoon, after they earlier urged people to evacuate for fear of potential health risks following a seafood processing plant fire in coastal Oregon.
articles.body: There was no further threat of ammonia contamination, officials said Sunday afternoon, after they earlier urged people to evacuate for fear of potential health risks following a seafood processing plant fire in coastal Oregon. Authorities responded to the blaze at Pacific Seafood, a major seafood processing and distribution plant, in the city of Newport’s Bayfront neighborhood just before 9 a.m., city spokesperson John Fuller said at an afternoon news conference. By 4 p.m. local time, officials said there was no threat of ammonia contamination. The Oregon State Fire Marshal said an ammonia tank had been found and that it didn’t seem to be punctured or leaking. Newport Fire Chief Rob Murphy said during the news conference that while trace amounts of ammonia were initially detected, there was no ongoing risk of ammonia exposure. “Between all the firefighters and our regional hazmat team, they did an excellent job of protecting those tanks and keeping them, you know, from something worse happening,” Murphy said. “I can tell you that the tanks are intact; they’re not leaking. The product inside them is stable and will remain so.” As of Sunday afternoon, he said the main environmental concern was smoke produced by the fire, which was still burning. There was still a small evacuation zone spanning blocks near the fire, he said. The blaze had earlier triggered “level 3” evacuations, meaning “extreme danger in the area,” for those within a 1-mile radius of the plant. Ammonia is a toxic clear gas or liquid, and exposure to high levels can hurt the skin, eyes, throat and lungs, while exposure to very high levels can cause lung damage or death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The city earlier recommended locals stay inside and wear a mask if outdoors. A shelter was set up at Atonement Lutheran Church for the displaced. Photos and video from the scene show heavy smoke rising from a blue-painted building and fire trucks dousing it with water. Fuller said no injuries were reported thus far and that there were 30 to 40 people in or near the facility at the time of the incident. He said that during peak tourist season in the summer, there can typically be as many as 200 people in the area. Newport Mayor Jan Kaplan described Pacific Seafood as a critical part of the city’s economy and a “significant employer.” The fire had erupted in a freezer facility where seafood is stored, and the blaze did not spread into the main plant, Fuller said. Ashton Meier, vice president of Pacific Seafood’s resource sales and processing, said in a statement that the company was “devastated” by the fire and expects “it will be a major loss.” “As a family-owned business, we deeply value our people and our community,” Meier said. “We are eternally grateful for the help of the emergency responders today and thank them for all of their efforts. We are incredibly thankful and glad to report that all of our team members on site are safe and accounted for and that at this time we are not aware of any injuries to others in the area.” Meier said the company work with public safety officials in determining the cause of the fire and any hazards.
