articles.title: Steve Hilton hits Dem governor's 2028 pitch by calling out Newsom's rail record
articles.summary: California Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton seized on Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear's boast about Democrat successes to criticize the struggling rail project under Gov. Gavin Newsom.
articles.body: Republican California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton challenged Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear's argument that a Democratic governor should lead the party's 2028 presidential ticket Friday on HBO's "Real Time with Bill Maher," pointing to California Gov. Gavin Newsom's unfinished high-speed rail project as Beshear touted Democratic governors' accomplishments. Beshear, discussing potential Democratic presidential contenders, argued that governors could point to tangible accomplishments that would distinguish them from President Donald Trump. "What Democratic governors have are receipts," he said. "You can look at, have you built the housing?" "Have you built the high-speed rail?" Hilton asked. BILL MAHER CLASHES WITH NEWSOM OVER CALIFORNIA LEADERS, SAYS OTHER SIDE WILL ASK, ‘HAVE YOU SEEN THE STATS?' The exchange came after Maher raised Newsom as a potential 2028 contender, although the California governor has not formally announced a presidential campaign. Maher acknowledged Hilton's point, suggesting the Republican candidate could use the project's troubled history against Newsom. "You're going to have a field day with that. No, you're right," Maher said. Matt Ciepielowski, Hilton's campaign manager, criticized California's continued investment in the project in a statement to Fox News Digital. "If Andy Beshear thinks California’s high-speed rail is something to brag about, he should try buying a ticket. Billions spent, years behind schedule, and Californians still can’t ride it. Gavin Newsom’s answer is to keep pouring money into it." Ciepielowski also said Hilton would end state funding for the project if elected governor. "Steve Hilton will end state funding on day one," he said. "Californians are struggling to pay their own bills. They shouldn’t have to keep paying for Sacramento’s failures, too." TRUMP BACKS HILTON AHEAD OF CALIFORNIA GOP VOTE, TESTING BIANCO’S GRIP ON PARTY ENDORSEMENT California state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach, vice chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, also criticized Newsom's handling of the project, pointing to findings about taxpayer-funded travel expenses submitted by project consultants. "The high-speed fail should have been defunded when Newsom took office in 2019," he said. "Instead, he doubled down on a project that will never be built as originally proposed to Californians. The latest scandal involving project consultants' misuse of public funds to pay for luxury travel under Newsom’s watch is yet another slap in the face to California families struggling to pay for essentials like gas, food, and rent." "These are taxpayer dollars, yet project consultants treat them like their personal ATM. This project will go down as one of the most wasteful government projects in California history," he continued. LIZ PEEK: CALIFORNIA VOTERS FED UP WITH DEMOCRATS MAY TURN TO STEVE HILTON FOR CHANGE California's high-speed rail system has faced years of delays and escalating costs since voters approved nearly $10 billion in bonds in 2008. An April estimate placed the cost of the full project at approximately $126 billion, compared with an original estimate of $33 billion. No high-speed track had been laid as of that report. The California High-Speed Rail Authority said in its 2026 business plan that completing the initial Merced-to-Bakersfield segment would cost an estimated $35.7 billion, with passenger service targeted for 2033. According to the authority's financial records, approximately $15.7 billion had been spent through February. The project's financial oversight also came under renewed scrutiny following a September investigation by California's independent high-speed rail inspector general. Investigators identified approximately $81,000 in consultant travel expenses that appeared to violate state regulations and another $543,000 that appeared impermissible under contract terms, with some overlap between the findings. Questionable charges included premium transportation and trips to gyms, a nightclub and an escape room. The California High-Speed Rail Authority outlined corrective actions, including additional oversight, employee training and efforts to recover payments determined to be improper. Despite the criticism, the California High-Speed Rail Authority has maintained that construction is advancing. In an October update, officials reported completing 66 major structures and nearly 90 miles of guideway in the Central Valley, while emphasizing the project's expected transportation, economic and employment benefits. articles.title: ‘The people have won’: Serbia’s Vucic concedes defeat after student-led protests win elections
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people flooded the streets of Serbia’s capital on Sunday night, bringing traffic to a halt and celebrating after long-time leader
articles.body: Tens of thousands of people flooded the streets of Serbia’s capital on Sunday night, bringing traffic to a halt and celebrating after long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in parliamentary elections to a student-backed opposition movement.Trams and vehicles were halted as crowds filled the city’s main boulevards, with smoke hanging in the air and supporters waving flares. The celebrations marked the culmination of a two-year protest movement that had called for Vucic to step down and for an end to what demonstrators described as rampant corruption — allegations the leader has denied.The election marks a major political shift in the Balkan country, where Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) had held power for 14 years. Vucic said his party’s projections showed the Students’ List winning between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-member Parliament, compared with around 105 for the SNS.“The Students’ List has won,” Vucic told supporters at his party’s election-night event. He blamed independent media, unnamed European countries and what he called an “American deep state” for the defeat.“That is the best thing that happened in my life. We will now breathe freely,” Milica, a law student, told Reuters said as supporters celebrated in Belgrade.Vucic had served as either prime minister or president since 2014 and presided over a period of strong economic growth. But his government faced mounting opposition after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The disaster triggered student-led protests over alleged corruption, cronyism and irregularities in renovation work.The Students’ List was shaped by university students, though students themselves did not appear on the electoral list. Instead, it fielded 250 candidates, including lawyers, professors, actors, farmers and other professionals, in an effort to challenge Vucic’s personalised style of rule and build a broader, non-partisan movement.At the movement’s headquarters, candidates and supporters embraced and cheered as the scale of their victory sank in.“The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!” said Nebojsa Cosic told Reuters, waving a flag in the street.The movement’s campaign focused on rebuilding the economy and restoring democracy, drawing support from voters disillusioned with established political parties. Supporters travelled by bicycle and on foot through the country to reach voters in rural areas that had traditionally backed Vucic.The election was closely watched by the European Union, as Serbia is a candidate for membership. Monitors reported dozens of suspected irregularities, including ballot photographing that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote-buying. International and local observers had also raised concerns about detentions, extensive government control over the media, and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks targeting activists.The student-backed victory echoed a recent electoral defeat for Vucic ally Viktor Orbán in Hungary and could resonate across Europe, where youth-led protests have challenged governments over political and economic grievances.The movement now faces the challenge of translating its electoral victory into government, while voters and international observers await the next steps in Serbia’s political transition.You use AI every day. articles.title: Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms
articles.summary: Demonstrators allege Prime Minister Andrej Babis and his coalition’s proposed reforms pose a threat to press freedom.
articles.body:
Several thousand people have taken to the streets in Prague to protest against plans to change the funding system for the Czech Republic’s public media, accusing the government of stifling press freedom.

On Sunday, protesters demanded the withdrawal of legislation seeking to abolish household licence fees and replace them with state budget allocations for public radio and television.

The Czech lower house of parliament approved fast-tracking the bill in a rare overnight vote on Saturday after governing coalition lawmakers rushed to open the issue, limiting the opposition’s ability to engage in debate before the vote was held.

The bill, proposed by the governing coalition led by billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis , which includes two far-right parties, must still be passed by the upper house before becoming law.

The opposition has pledged to challenge the legislation in the constitutional court. The plan would cut funding for public media by about 15 percent, possibly as early as next year.

At the protest in Prague’s Old Town Square, demonstrators chanted, “We’ve had enough”, “This must not be allowed to pass”, and “4:36”, referencing the early morning hour when the draft was approved by parliament.

Babis has said the plan is not an attack on media independence but a matter of funding transparency.

Critics warn the proposed change would allow the governing coalition to take control of the media. They compare it with the actions of populist governments , such as Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico.

Babis and his coalition, whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion, have a record of attacks against the media.

Public media staffers announced they would go on strike on November 3. They are backed by labour unions, university rectors, churches, international media organisations and many others.

A rally is also planned at Prague’s Letna park on November 15, two days before the anniversary of the 1989 anti-communist Velvet Revolution that ended more than 40 years of totalitarian government.

articles.title: From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming
articles.summary: From remote monitoring of cattle to automation of processes that took up valuable time, farmers in NI are rapidly becoming skilled in technology.
articles.body:
George McMaster's farming career started with milking eight cows in a byre, relying on his eyes to spot any health issues in his cattle.

He still watches his now-300-strong herd, but via a feed from an AI camera in the milking parlour at the farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim.

The device uses an algorithm which assigns each cow its own ID, records a short video of the animal every day, analyses it and flags any changes - often before they are visible to the human eye.

For the third generation farmer, it is "absolutely incredible to move from all hand-done to sitting on the phone, watching what's happening outside".

It is just one example of how technology is changing the traditional profession.

George's son Jack, who is taking over the farm, jumped at the chance to get involved with the CattleEye app when a local developer approached him.

He, too, is astonished by the potential.

"There's cows there we would never have thought of as lame when we were just watching them every day, but whenever the camera's watching they're picking them up so much earlier, any emergencies that we have, to check cows before they lose condition and get sick," he said.

"And if cows are in better health, we get more milk and they're happier - happy cows make happy farmers."

Caleb Howard is using technology to manage his 90 Jersey cows on the farm near Coagh in County Tyrone.

They filter in and out of a robotic milking machine when they want to, rather than being herded in at set times.

Like the McMasters, he thinks "everything is going down the robotic route" to improve efficiency.

But historically in a place like rural Tyrone, that has come with its own challenges.

Getting high-speed broadband was a game-changer for him - he has been able to open a farm shop with an electronic payment system.

"Ten years ago, in our area, phone signal was rubbish, the broadband wasn't great, it was just like a slightly faster dial-up," he said.

"So now everything is much simpler and much easier-used when you've got a good internet connection."

Project Stratum was set up to deliver high-speed broadband to areas like the one Howard lives in.

Colin Hutchinson from Fibrus, which delivered the project, said it had had a "massive" economic impact.

"Being online and having good broadband access is really crucial now," he said.

"And it's enabling businesses like this to thrive in really rural locations."

Robert Smyth runs a herd of 100 dairy cows in another rural location, near Randalstown in County Antrim.

For four years now, he has used the FarmDrive app to run the business.

"It's so much handier - beforehand you're writing things down, bits of paperwork in the cattle house and writing them down in the office, whereas now you just do it at that time," he said.

"And then whenever you have inspections coming up, all you have to do is go into your compliance section, select reports, and there's your reports for your medicine, for your meal records, for everything.

"The AI really should be looking towards how to manage your farm better and how to reduce your inputs and increase your outputs."

Developer Gareth McDonald describes FarmDrive as "Facebook for cows". Each animal gets a profile with all her records in one place and a photo can be added.

He comes from a farming background and studied computer science.

Although he is passionate about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans.

"It's allowing us to work a lot more quickly and efficiently, and on the farming side, it's basically allowing the farmer to see the right information at the right time, where it's kind of that adviser to the farmer," he said.

"We're very much of the opinion we don't want the AI making the decision for the farmer."

Almost a century ago, County Down-born inventor Harry Ferguson transformed the farming industry when he developed the linkage system still used in tractors today.

Former president of the Ulster Farmers' Union Ian Marshall says AI is similarly revolutionary.

While the industry has always relied on data, he believes technology will drive how information is used.

"When we take all the datasets, then I think we can deliver on the three pillars of sustainability - economic, environmental and social," he said.

"So I think that because we've got so much data and so much digitalisation in the industry, that farmers will certainly use this to their advantage and can meet their targets, meet their objectives and meet the obligations whilst delivering good quality, sustainable food."

articles.title: Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
articles.summary: Leftist president mounts stunning comeback after unexpected first round loss galvanised supporters of Flavio Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right.

Around 9:13pm Brasilia time (00:13 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned 51 percent of the vote, with more than 96 percent of ballots counted.

More than 51.49 million ballots were cast for the incumbent. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48.68 percent of the vote, or 48.8 million ballots.

No other candidate in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election, only to win the second round.

Still, the vote process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, after reports emerged that public transportation in some areas had been suspended.

With heavy rain affecting other parts of the country, the campaigns of both Lula and Bolsonaro petitioned the Supreme Court for a voting extension. Polls across the country were kept open two hours later than expected, until 7pm Brasilia time (22:00 GMT).

Sunday’s victory means that Lula will retain the presidency of the largest country in Latin America, denying a crucial victory to the region’s right wing.

In recent years, right-wing leaders have swept presidential races in nearby countries like Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Many have ridden a wave of anti-incumbent energy and have enjoyed support from United States President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025.

A former union leader for metalworkers, Lula — at age 80 — will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, when he will beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to take the oath of office since the country’s return to democracy.

His victory has earned him an unprecedented fourth non-consecutive term in office.

Lula came into Sunday’s runoff as an underdog, however. While he narrowly led in pre-election, the first round of voting on October 4 showed him trailing Bolsonaro.

He earned 45 percent of the first round vote, compared to the right-wing senator’s 47 percent — both tallies short of the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff.

But in the weeks since, Lula has rallied supporters around cost-of-living issues. He championed a constitutional amendment passed this month that shortened the Brazilian workweek, and he floated the possibility of providing free public transportation on weekends.

Having entered politics in the 1980s, during the twilight of the country’s military dictatorship, Lula has run for president seven times.

He won two consecutive terms from 2002 through 2010, as well as a third term in 2022, in what was the tightest race in modern Brazilian history up to that point.

His rival in that election, former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, is father to Senator Bolsonaro, his adversary in this race.

Jair Bolsonaro has since been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in plotting a coup plot following his loss to Lula.

Despite overseeing a decline in poverty and low unemployment during his third term in office, Lula has faced questions about his age, his ability to combat crime, and the country’s polarised political landscape.

An explosion of household indebtedness has also left many Brazilians feeling that their economic circumstances had worsened.

In September, Lula banned online gambling and sports betting apps, in a bid to address the issue.

While the victory over Bolsonaro cements Lula’s status as one of the most significant and influential figures in Brazil’s modern history, efforts to advance legislative priorities during his fourth term could be stymied by the most right-wing Congress in recent memory.
